section.title: Ways in
section.intro: There are more ways into work than the CAO. Some pay you from the first year, some cost almost nothing, and some are available years after you leave school. These pages explain how each one actually works.

items.title: Apprenticeships
items.subtitle: Earn while you learn
items.summary: You're employed from day one, paid a wage that rises each year, and you finish with a recognised qualification and no student debt.
items.body:
An apprenticeship is a job with structured training attached. You are an employee from the first day, paid a wage, and you alternate between working and blocks of off-the-job training. At the end you hold a nationally recognised qualification.

The part most students are never told: apprenticeships are no longer just trades. There are apprenticeships in software, finance, insurance, engineering, logistics, hospitality and accountancy — some leading to degree-level qualifications.

blocks.heading: The hard part is finding an employer
blocks.text: This is the real barrier, and it's why this website exists. You aren't applying through a central system the way you would with the CAO — you're finding a company willing to take you on. Ringing local firms directly works more often than people expect. Knowing somebody helps, which is exactly the gap we're trying to close.

blocks.heading: If you can't find one yet
blocks.text: A pre-apprenticeship or PLC course in the same field gives you practical experience and makes an employer far more likely to say yes. It is not a step backwards.

blocks.heading: There's no age limit
blocks.text: People start apprenticeships in their twenties, thirties and later, often after working in something else entirely. It is not a decision you have to make at seventeen or never.

blocks.heading: Where it leads
blocks.text: Qualified tradespeople move into supervision, contracting, inspection, teaching, and running their own businesses. Self-employment is a realistic route, and many earn more than graduates in office jobs.

myths.myth: Apprenticeships are for people who aren't academic.
myths.reality: The exams are real and people fail them. It's a different kind of difficulty, not a lesser one.
Software, insurance, finance, accountancy, engineering and logistics all have apprenticeships. Most students are never told this.

myths.myth: You'll earn less in the long run.
myths.reality: You start earning four years earlier and finish with no debt. That head start is bigger than people assume.

items.title: PLC and further education
items.subtitle: No points, low fees, a second chance
items.summary: A one or two year course with no points requirement, very low fees, and a route onward to either work or a degree.
items.body:
A Post Leaving Certificate course is a practical, full-time course run by an Education and Training Board or further education college. You apply directly to the college rather than through the CAO, and there is no points requirement.

They are often described as a fallback. That framing does students a disservice. A PLC is a legitimate route in its own right, it leads directly to employment in many fields, and it is also one of the most reliable ways into a degree for someone whose Leaving Certificate did not go the way they hoped.

blocks.heading: It's a route to a degree, not a dead end
blocks.text: Completing a PLC can get you into higher education through progression arrangements between further education colleges and universities. For some courses this is an easier path to the same degree than competing on points at eighteen. Ask the college specifically which higher education courses their students progress to.

blocks.heading: You apply directly, and later than the CAO
blocks.text: There is no central system and no single deadline. You contact the college or ETB, and many accept applications well into the summer - including after Leaving Certificate results, which matters if things did not go to plan.

blocks.heading: The classes are smaller and the work is practical
blocks.text: Assessment tends to be continuous rather than one set of exams. For students who did not suit the Leaving Certificate format, this alone can change the outcome.

blocks.heading: It's also a way into an apprenticeship
blocks.text: A PLC in a relevant field gives you practical experience and makes an employer far more likely to take you on as an apprentice.

myths.myth: It's what you do if you fail.
myths.reality: It's what a lot of people do who end up with the same degree by a different road - and some who prefer the qualification itself.
QQI awards are nationally recognised, and in many fields the practical training is exactly what an employer wants.
Probably not. Many colleges take applications through the summer.

items.title: CAO and college
items.subtitle: The route everyone's told about
items.summary: The one your school explains. Worth knowing the parts they usually leave out - reduced points entry, starting at a lower level, and that none of it is final.
items.body:
The Central Applications Office handles applications to almost all higher education courses in Ireland. You list courses in order of preference, your Leaving Certificate results convert to points, and offers are made in rounds.

Your school will explain this part. What often goes unmentioned is how much flexibility exists inside it.

blocks.heading: You may not need the points everyone quotes
blocks.text: HEAR offers places on reduced points to students from socio-economically disadvantaged backgrounds, and if you are in a DEIS school there is a real chance you qualify. It is applied for through the CAO, with an earlier deadline than the main one. This is the single most useful thing on this website and most students who could use it never apply.

blocks.heading: You can start at a lower level and move up
blocks.text: Level 6 and Level 7 courses take far fewer points than Level 8 honours degrees, and many allow you to progress into the degree afterwards. Getting to the same place a year later is still getting there.

blocks.heading: Nothing you choose at seventeen is final
blocks.text: People transfer course, repeat a year, drop out and return, or come back years later as mature students - entry at twenty-three is assessed on your circumstances rather than your Leaving Certificate. Treating the CAO form as a life sentence causes more harm than any course choice on it.

blocks.heading: Money is usually the smaller problem
blocks.text: Between SUSI, the 1916 Bursary and college access funds, the cost is reduced or covered for a great many students. Work out the money question separately from the course question, and do not rule out a course before you have checked.

myths.myth: The points are the standard of the course.
myths.reality: Points are just supply and demand. A high-points course is popular, not necessarily better.

myths.myth: I have to go straight after school.
myths.reality: Mature entry at twenty-three exists precisely because plenty of people don't.

myths.myth: If I don't get my first choice I've failed.
myths.reality: Most people don't get their first choice. Transfers, progression and postgraduate routes all exist.

items.title: Studying in Europe
items.subtitle: Often cheaper than staying home
items.summary: English-taught degrees across Europe at EU fee rates — frequently a fraction of what the same degree costs in the UK, and sometimes less than in Ireland.
items.body:
As an Irish citizen you are an EU student, which means you pay the same tuition as a local student in any EU country. In several countries that is far less than you would pay in the UK, and hundreds of degrees are taught entirely in English.

The Netherlands is the best-known route for Irish students — a large number of English-taught bachelor's degrees, an established application system, and a student culture used to international arrivals. Germany and the Nordic countries also teach in English at low or no tuition cost.

Almost nobody in an Irish school mentions this. It is a real option, and for some courses it is both cheaper and easier to get into than the Irish equivalent.

blocks.heading: Why it isn't the UK
blocks.text: Since Brexit, fee arrangements for Irish students in the UK have changed and vary. Check the current position carefully before assuming anything. Continental Europe is the more reliable value, and the reason this page focuses there.

blocks.heading: Entry can work differently
blocks.text: Many European universities don't use a points race the way the CAO does. Some courses admit anyone meeting a minimum requirement; others use a lottery or their own selection. A course that is out of reach on points in Ireland may not be abroad.

blocks.heading: Housing is the real difficulty
blocks.text: Not fees — accommodation. In Dutch cities especially, student housing is scarce and must be arranged early. This is the thing that catches people out, and it is worth planning before you accept a place.

blocks.heading: You can still get Irish support
blocks.text: Some Irish student supports apply to study elsewhere in the EU, and some don't. Check with SUSI directly rather than guessing — the answer depends on the course and country.

blocks.heading: What you get beyond the degree
blocks.text: Living in another country in your late teens changes what you think is possible, and employers notice it. For a student who has not travelled much, this is arguably the biggest part of the value.

myths.reality: Hundreds of degrees across Europe are taught entirely in English, particularly in the Netherlands and the Nordics.

myths.myth: It must be more expensive than home.
myths.reality: EU tuition rates are often lower than the Irish student contribution. Living costs vary — sometimes higher, sometimes not.

myths.myth: An Irish employer won't recognise it.
myths.reality: EU degrees are recognised across the EU. It's a normal qualification, not an exotic one.
